title: Beating Boredom: Two Tactics, Two Thoughts
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart reviews Martha Sevetson Rush's book Beat Boredom and extracts two classroom-ready tactics — using storytelling as a lesson hook and framing lessons or units toward an end-of-unit discussion or debate — as evidence-backed strategies for reducing unproductive student disengagement. He then raises two broader analytical thoughts. First, he distinguishes between unproductive boredom, which should be reduced, and purposeful boredom, which James Clear and Cal Newport argue must be embraced for deep skill development — warning that teachers should not take Rush's book as a mandate against all boredom. Second, he adds a structural critique: much student disengagement stems not from classroom failures but from years of incoherent, knowledge-light curricula that leave students without the prior knowledge needed to perceive themselves as capable learners. The article holds teacher-level intervention and systemic curriculum reform as equally necessary, insisting that the best minds in education must address both simultaneously.
points: Storytelling before a text or lesson is an evidence-backed interest hook — the mind is structured for narrative, and Martha Rush's chapter reinforces what cognitive scientist Dan Willingham also argues.
Framing a lesson or unit toward an upcoming discussion or debate reliably elevates student interest throughout the learning arc, not just at the moment of the activity itself.

Not all boredom is bad: James Clear and Cal Newport both argue that tolerating purposeful, productive boredom is a prerequisite for building real skill — the target is unproductive and frustrating boredom, not all boredom.

Much student disengagement is rooted in structural curriculum failures — years of incoherent, knowledge-lite instruction leave students without the prior knowledge that generates perceived competence and motivation.
The link between prior knowledge and motivation is commonsensical but underappreciated: students approach work in domains they know well with higher confidence, a core driver of the Efficacy belief.
quotes: Martha was one of those second-career teachers that exudes a passion for the work. After college, she had been a journalist, but once she started covering schools, her mind couldn't stop spinning with the possibilities of the classroom.
Whenever I say to my students, "At the end of our study here, we're going to have a debate on X prompt," their interest rises.

Martha's book isn't opposed to these ideas. Rather, she's taking issue with pointless and frustrating boredom, while Clear and Newport advocate for an embrace of purposeful, rewarding boredom. This distinction is critical.

One thing I struggle with is that, though the demotivation our students experience is influenceable at the level of our classrooms, much of it is rooted in broken systems. Yes, your students' engagement can be influenced (via the Five Key Beliefs) in the context of your classroom, but if your students have experienced an incoherent, nonsequential, knowledge-lite curricula during the five years preceding your classroom, then your students' level of prior knowledge will affect their motivation.

When I approach work in an area that I know much about, I'll be more likely to think I can succeed at that work than I will in an area that I know little about — the link between prior knowledge and motivation is commonsensical when I put it that way but remarkably underappreciated in much of our professional discourse.

we've got to do what we can to, as Martha puts it, beat unproductive, frustrating boredom. But we've also got to start getting our best minds on the problem of shoddy, incoherent, siloed K-12 curricula.
